article_title: Science Teachers Learning from Lesson Analysis (STeLLA)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, May). Science Teachers Learning through Lesson Analysis (STeLLA®). https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Analysis-of-practice videocase-based professional development with school-based study groups
description: STeLLA®'s core design pattern is analysis of practice: teachers learn a lesson analysis process at a summer institute by discussing videos of experienced teachers, then during the school year videorecord themselves teaching and analyze one another's videorecorded lessons and student work in school-based study groups. In the first half of the year teachers analyze videos of one another delivering model lesson plans; in the second half they collaboratively develop their own lesson plans incorporating STeLLA® teaching strategies and anticipating student misconceptions, then deliver, videorecord, and analyze these lessons.
requirements: A STeLLA® professional development leader works with school-based study groups
Monthly discussion sessions each lasting 3 to 4 hours during the school year
constraints: Study group meetings take place at participating schools, with the professional development leader joining online or on-site depending on availability of local leaders
target_learners: Elementary teachers of science in grades 4 and 5 (in the studied implementation)
target_learning_goals: Learning to convey science content to students
Implementing STeLLA® teaching strategies in teachers' own classrooms
examples: Teachers receive transcripts of program-developed videorecorded lessons and related examples of student work, and BSCS provides online access to videorecordings made by members of their local study group
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, May). Science Teachers Learning through Lesson Analysis (STeLLA®). https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/716

article_title: The Unintended Consequences of an Algebra-for-All Policy on High-Skill Students
citation: Algebra-for-all policy in Chicago: effects on classroom academic composition and high-skill students' math achievement. (2012). Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 34(4). https://journals.sagepub.com/
title: Anticipate how schools reorganize classrooms in response to curricular mandates, because organizational responses can harm untargeted students
description: This principle holds that curricular policies such as algebra-for-all should be evaluated not only on their targeted participants but on how schools reorganize classrooms to comply. The study finds that "schools created more mixed-ability classrooms when eliminating remedial math classes," which lowered peer skill for high-skill students and, consequently, their test scores. Policy design should therefore account for composition spillovers onto students the policy does not target.
requirements: Analysis of a curricular mandate must include how schools organize classrooms to accommodate the curricular change, since little was known about this response.
constraints: Evidence comes from one district (Chicago) and one policy (1997 algebra-for-all for ninth grade), using an interrupted time-series design with within-cohort comparisons.
target_learning_goals: Algebra / mathematics achievement
examples: Chicago's 1997 policy required algebra for all ninth-graders and eliminated remedial coursework; schools responded by mixing ability levels within algebra classrooms.
key_sources: Algebra-for-all policy in Chicago: effects on classroom academic composition and high-skill students' math achievement. (2012). Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 34(4). https://journals.sagepub.com/

article_title: The Chicago Annenberg Challenge
citation: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Network structure: clusters of at least three like-minded schools aided by an external partner, restructuring time, size, and isolation
description: The Chicago Annenberg Challenge's core design pattern required schools to apply not individually but in networks—clusters of at least three like-minded schools aided by an external partner—to enhance collaboration and community support. Grantees were asked to focus on how they might "alter the basic elements of time, size, and isolation": reorganizing the school day, creating smaller personalized environments, and connecting educators to the communities they serve. External partners were intended to provide community resources, develop the pool of assisting organizations, and build adult leadership at schools.
requirements: At least three schools per cluster; an external partner for each network; a rich invitational application process
constraints: Funds were stipulated not to go to the CPS central administration; the pattern was grounded in the 1988 decentralization context
target_learners: students and educators in Chicago Public Schools network schools
target_learning_goals: school restructuring to improve students' opportunities to learn through collaboration and community support
examples: The Working Group's proposal required implementation-grant clusters of at least three schools with external partners, and first-year grantees were selected largely from existing school-partner collaborations
key_sources: Dorothy Shipps, Karin Sconzert, with Holly Swyers. (1999). The Chicago Annenberg Challenge: The First Three Years. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/chicago-annenberg-challenge-first-three-years

article_title: Understanding the Initial Educational Impacts of COVID-19 on Communities of Color
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Erik Ruzek, Karyn Lewis, Jim Soland, Angela Johnson, Beth Tarasawa, & Lindsay Dworkin. (2021). Understanding the initial educational impacts of COVID-19 on communities of color. NWEA Research Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Analyze achievement equity without centering whiteness as the default comparison standard
description: The report's authors, in line with Critical Race and Critical Whiteness Theorists, explicitly chose to exclude White students from their analyses to avoid centering whiteness as the default academic standard, instead comparing BIPOC students' pandemic-era performance to same-race/ethnicity students' pre-pandemic performance. They also acknowledge the risk that enumerating inequities adopts a deficit-based perspective that perpetuates a victim-blaming orientation, and state that focus should be on dominant power systems rather than fixing BIPOC students.
requirements: Comparisons must be framed against same-race/ethnicity pre-pandemic baselines rather than against White students as the reference group
constraints: The authors note this descriptive framing does not by itself explain why gains were lower; their data cannot speak to why academic gains were lower during the pandemic
target_learners: Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC) students
target_learning_goals: Equitable interpretation and monitoring of academic achievement and growth
examples: The report adopted the gender-neutral term Latinx and compared students to same race/ethnic peers before and after the pandemic rather than to White students
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, Erik Ruzek, Karyn Lewis, Jim Soland, Angela Johnson, Beth Tarasawa, & Lindsay Dworkin. (2021). Understanding the initial educational impacts of COVID-19 on communities of color. article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Anchor adult learning design in learners' past experience and life relevance
description: The report's first principle holds that "At the heart of all of theories about how adults learn is the notion of experience." Learning succeeds when adults connect new information to past experience or see its relevance to their lives, so products should let learners do something with new knowledge in practical, authentic tasks.
requirements: Authentic activities must include "a variety of perspectives and examples so students will find something they can relate to and connect with."
constraints: Designers cannot assume a common background: "there is no one typical adult learner experience to rely on."
target_learners: adult learners with varied educational and employment backgrounds
target_learning_goals: connecting new information to prior experience
vocabulary and skills for real tasks such as job applications
examples: USA Learns teaches job-application vocabulary "in the context of a sample job application," ending with students filling out an application for a real job; other named strategies include role-playing, simulations, case studies, and games.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments: Evaluation Final Report
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Analysis-of-practice vPLC session pattern: teacher-shared stories, breakout discussion grounded in teachers' own classrooms, and peer-to-peer exchange
description: The vPLC's reusable session pattern is grounded in "the analysis-of-practice model, an evidence-based approach to improving instruction through collaborative reflection (Taylor et al., 2017)". Each session opens with norms and an icebreaker, features a Story From the Field in which a participating teacher shares a real instructional experience, moves through facilitator-led concept introduction or platform demonstration, then small-group discussion referencing teachers' own classrooms, assignments, and student data, and closes with informal peer Q&A and reflection.
requirements: Facilitators experienced in using ASSISTments and a facilitation guide grounded in best practices for professional learning are needed to run the sessions.
constraints: The format is participant-driven and responsive, with teachers actively shaping each session by contributing their own practices and pedagogical insights.
target_learners: Practicing middle school math teachers, including those in rural or professionally isolated settings
target_learning_goals: Collaborative reflection on instruction and integration of ASSISTments into classroom routines
examples: Feedback from teacher surveys informed continuous improvements, including integrating community norms, tone-setting activities, icebreakers, and shared reports across sessions.

article_title: Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers
citation: Howard Ziyu Han, Nikolas Martelaro. (2026). Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04166
title: Antagonistic AI design agent with steerable stakeholder pushback in Miro
description: An LLM-powered agent built in Miro (Next.js, Miro SDK, GPT-4.1, Whisper, GPT-4o) that enacts constructive conflict for interaction design students. In the Agent Intervention Space, "the agent generates a first round of four pushback points anchored in the designer's current proposal; the designer interacts with those points to steer the design direction; the agent then generates a second round informed by that steering." Each pushback point pairs a stakeholder perspective with a specific challenge. Designers steer via point-level tagging (useful, not useful, custom) and stance-level Consensus and Command frames. A sub-agent retrieves a database of prior constructive-conflict examples to ground critiques.
requirements: Multimodal context gathering (text, visuals, think-aloud) so pushback is anchored in the designer's contextual exploration
Steering mechanisms (tagging and Consensus/Command frames) so designers retain agency while engaging with critique
constraints: The agent could not infer relationships between linked ideas from think-aloud input
It cannot show how common, important, or grounded synthetic concerns are in lived experience and does not substitute for engagement with the real public
A few Miro actions not exposed by the open API were handled by the researcher via a predefined, bias-avoiding protocol
target_learners: Novice interaction designers (design students trained in interaction design but novices at navigating stakeholder conflict)
target_learning_goals: Engaging constructively with multi-stakeholder tension during early design ideation
Reconsidering and revising design decisions in light of stakeholder pushback
examples: In the study, the agent raised the concern that community members might feel their efforts were devalued when tickets are merged, and a participant revised the automatic-merge idea accordingly
key_sources: Howard Ziyu Han, Nikolas Martelaro. (2026). Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04166

article_title: ANVIL: Analogies and Videos for Lecturers
citation: Noviello, Y., Birillo, A., Migut, G. (2026). ANVIL: Analogies and Videos for Lecturers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16295
title: ANVIL: a three-layer generative pipeline producing analogy-based manim animations with an agentic repair loop
description: ANVIL (ANalogies and VIdeos for Lecturers) is an open-source system that automates end-to-end production of analogy-based instructional animations for CS concepts. It "employs a staged pipeline that generates an analogy (Textual Layer), compiles it into a structured visual screenplay (Screenplay Layer), and generates executable Python manim code". A bounded diagnose-repair-verify loop capped at n=3 iterations recovers from code-generation failures without human intervention, and all intermediate artifacts are saved for inspection and reuse.
requirements: Requires LLM backends for each layer (the paper used gpt-4o for Textual and Screenplay Layers and claude-3.7-sonnet for the Code Layer) and a concept definition as input
constraints: LLM-generated manim code can fail due to API hallucinations, syntax errors, or inconsistent object references, which the repair loop addresses
Repair is invoked only if errors are detected and the loop is capped at n=3 iterations
target_learners: CS/SE educators creating materials for novice learners of algorithms, data structures, and software patterns
target_learning_goals: Understanding of abstract CS concepts through analogy-based visual explanations
examples: For each of nine CS topics, participants were shown the target concept definition, the generated textual analogy, and the corresponding rendered animation
key_sources: Noviello, Y., Birillo, A., Migut, G. (2026). ANVIL: Analogies and Videos for Lecturers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16295

article_title: When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills
citation: Yongli Xiang, Zhifang Zhang, Bojun Yang, Ziming Hong, Lei Feng, Miao Xu, Tongliang Liu. (2026). When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700
title: AntiSkillBench: an end-to-end benchmark for persona-skill privacy and impersonation risks
description: AntiSkillBench is a benchmark that evaluates risks and defenses across the persona-skill pipeline. It comprises "a dataset of 7,500 persona-grounded dialogue traces, constructed from 50 behaviorally rich profiles spanning diverse task scenarios", an evaluation suite measuring skill-level privacy leakage and agent-level attribute disclosure and behavioral impersonation, and a defense evaluation covering online and post-hoc interventions. Profiles are organized into demographics, background, personality, and communication dimensions, with 50 persona-grounded questions per user expanded into three-round dialogues.
requirements: Requires persona-grounded user profiles and simulated multi-turn dialogue traces as input for skill distillation
constraints: Traces are simulated user-assistant dialogues rather than real user histories
target_learners: LLM-based agent systems and their developers
target_learning_goals: Evaluating privacy leakage and impersonation risk in personalized agent skills
examples: 50 user roles each paired with 50 generated questions and expanded into three-round dialogues, yielding 2,500 dialogue traces comprising 7,500 persona-grounded user turns
key_sources: Yongli Xiang, Zhifang Zhang, Bojun Yang, Ziming Hong, Lei Feng, Miao Xu, Tongliang Liu. (2026). When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700

article_title: Anticipatory governance and leadership for AI implementation in higher education: A scoping review
citation: Sandra Baroudi. (2026). Anticipatory governance and leadership for AI implementation in higher education: A scoping review. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00616-7
title: Anticipatory governance as a proactive, participatory, adaptive decision-making framework for higher education facing AI-driven futures
description: The review adopts anticipatory governance as its main theoretical framework, defining it as "a proactive, participatory, and adaptive deci-sion-making model that calls upon educational leaders to engage with uncertain futures". It rests on foresight tools, stakeholder co-creation, and flexible, inclusive policy frameworks to shape possible futures rather than react to crises. The framework distinguishes anticipatory leadership (the micro-level mindset and actions operationalising it) from AI governance (the ethical, policy, and regulatory mechanisms guiding responsible AI use), with participatory governance as a key dimension. Required competencies named include imagination, systems thinking, ethical reasoning, and technological and AI literacy.
requirements: Stakeholder co-creation and engagement of leaders, educators, students, and communities who collaboratively imagine, experiment, and learn iteratively
Data analytics to inform strategic decisions and policies
Foresight tools and flexible, inclusive policy frameworks
constraints: The review states it must be adapted to institutional, cultural, and infrastructure conditions of different regions rather than applied as a universal framework
It must go beyond managerial rationales and ground itself in participatory and inclusive leadership
target_learning_goals: Preparing institutions for AI-driven transformation
Building foresight, ethical reasoning, and AI literacy
Fostering inclusive, equitable governance of educational technology
examples: The review cites Finland's strategic foresight and scenario-based policy-making in sport education programs, and Egypt's Egyptian Knowledge Bank and free digital access initiatives as early examples of anticipatory governance in action
key_sources: Sandra Baroudi. (2026). Anticipatory governance and leadership for AI implementation in higher education: A scoping review. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00616-7

article_title: Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts’ Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images
citation: Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, Matthew Groh. (2026). Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts' Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28510
title: Analyst image-detection open code, data, and stimulus release
description: The article releases the study's code, de-identified data, and stimulus images through a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/negarkamali/analyst-image-detection). The release includes "all stimulus images (50 AI-generated images and 47 real photographs)" from the deployed 97-image evaluation set, which was balanced across authenticity, scene complexity, and matched real–fake image-to-text description pairs. The stimulus set was drawn from a larger pool of 149 verified real photographs and 450 photorealistic AI-generated images used in previous deepfake-detection research, making it reusable for training and evaluation studies on human discrimination of diffusion-model imagery.
requirements: Stimulus images balanced with respect to authenticity, scene complexity, and image-to-text descriptions to support controlled experiments
constraints: The study examines photorealistic still images from diffusion models only; it does not examine AI-generated video or audio
target_learners: researchers studying human detection of AI-generated media
target_learning_goals: evaluating human ability to distinguish real from AI-generated images
designing and replicating training interventions on artifact-based visual discrimination
examples: The counterbalanced experiment collected 2,544 image-level judgments from 32 intelligence analysts using this stimulus set
key_sources: Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, Matthew Groh. (2026). Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts' Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28510

article_title: Multimodal Examination Answer Data with Expert-Designed Outcome-Based Education Rubrics for Criterion-Level Assessment
citation: Jahangir Alam SM, Md Khalid Syfullaha, Saad Ahmed, Munira Akter Mou, A K Z Rasel Rahman, A.K.M. Masudur Rahman, Mohammed Sowket Ali. (2026). Multimodal examination answer data with expert-designed Outcome-Based Education rubrics for criterion-level assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22346
title: Answer-level JSON record linking a randomized scan to question, model answer, and rubric criteria with performance-level marking rules
description: Each dataset record is one JSON object paired with one randomized PDF filename. The object stores answer_id, pdf_file, Subject, question, model_answer, and total_marks, plus a variable-length rubrics array whose elements store criterion text, gained_marks, and marking_rules. "The four performance keys areExcellent,Good,Average, andPoor." This structure keeps grading context next to the file reference and supports answer-level loading without joining separate tables.
requirements: One-to-one mapping between each metadata object and one scanned PDF
Rubric objects stored as arrays to preserve question-specific criterion counts
constraints: Performance labels are descriptive guidance, not a substitute for the criterion maximum
target_learners: higher education students assessed under OBE frameworks
target_learning_goals: criterion-level automated grading
evidence-grounded feedback generation
score prediction research
examples: The rubrics field is a variable-length array whose length equals the number of criteria defined for the associated question

article_title: MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-Modal Understanding in Situated Education
citation: Luyao Zhu, Xun Wei Yee, Wei Li, Mun Thye Mak, Wee Siong Ng. (2026). MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-modal Understanding in Situated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19088
title: Annotation-first, task-generative benchmark construction framework
description: MUSE's construction framework separates what an image contains from how a capability is queried: "each artwork is annotated once with a reusable structured representation of its visual and semantic content, after which task-specific questions are instantiated through predefined generation rules." This decoupling supports annotation reuse across tasks, consistent semantics between independently generated tasks, and explicit control over question format and difficulty, while reducing the annotation effort required to extend a benchmark to new tasks.
requirements: A shared structured visual-semantic annotation per image, plus predefined generation rules per task
constraints: Difficulty control requires explicit modeling of reasoning structure, per prior work the authors cite on controllable question generation
target_learners: benchmark builders and educational AI developers
target_learning_goals: reliable evaluation of multi-modal understanding capabilities for educational applications
examples: One artwork supports the full 12-task suite, including a four-turn affective sequence (Object Classification, Emotion Detection, Visual Clue Identification, Emotion Cause Inference) with earlier turns retained in dialogue history
key_sources: Luyao Zhu, Xun Wei Yee, Wei Li, Mun Thye Mak, Wee Siong Ng. (2026). MUSE: Benchmarking Large Vision-Language Models on Multi-modal Understanding in Situated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19088

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Annotated decision trails as integrity artefacts documenting evaluative decisions about GenAI contributions
description: Annotated decision trails invite learners to document how GenAI contributed to their work and why particular outputs were retained, modified, or rejected in relation to disciplinary criteria. The paper describes them as "integrity artefacts, documenting how learners navigate responsibility within hybrid human-GenAI systems", rendering ethical decision-making observable without surveillance technologies. They also address equity by holding all learners accountable for articulating judgement regardless of language proficiency.
requirements: Scalability in larger enrolment contexts is supported by focused annotation of selected decision points and rubric criteria attending to quality of reasoning rather than volume of reflection
constraints: The paper offers these as illustrative rather than evidentiary mechanisms, not comprehensive pedagogical frameworks
target_learners: higher education students using GenAI tools
target_learning_goals: transparent disclosure of evaluative reasoning and accountability for academic decisions
examples: Appendix A models the practice reflexively, documenting the author's decisions to accept or reject ChatGPT5 revision suggestions during manuscript preparation
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Integrating LLM with consortium blockchain for personalized and verifiable online education in higher education
citation: Fuan Xiao, Jiahui Huang, Jia-Xin Huang, Huali Ren and Lang Li. (2026). Integrating LLM with consortium blockchain for personalized and verifiable online education in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00618-5
title: Anchor LLM inference provenance on-chain and require instructor co-signatures for high-stakes grading records
description: To make AI-generated educational decisions auditable and attributable, the framework records not only the AI output but the full inference configuration on the consortium ledger: "the model release and inference configuration (model/checkpoint ID, prompt-template hash, decoding parameters, and random seed, etc.) as hashed records on a consortium blockchain". High-stakes records such as final grades and certificates carry both an AI service signature and an instructor co-signature, and any later override is appended as a linked, traceable transaction rather than overwriting history.
requirements: The AI service must sign its outputs and the smart contract must enforce the hybrid AI-plus-instructor signing protocol for important records
constraints: Applies to key grading outcomes; low-risk tutoring interactions are not recorded on-chain
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: accountable and reproducible automated assessment
examples: The prototype anchors model/checkpoint ID, prompt-template hash, decoding parameters, and random seed as hashed on-chain records and requires instructor co-signatures for key grading outcomes

article_title: Knowledge elaboration: A cognitive load perspective
citation: Ramírez Ruiz, J. J. (2018). Efecto de un andamiaje de autoeficacia en el estilo cognitivo, el logro de aprendizaje y la carga cognitiva. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://bibliotecadigital.upn.edu.co
title: Incorporar andamiajes motivacionales de autoeficacia en ambientes computacionales para favorecer logro equitativo entre estilos cognitivos
description: Principio de diseño derivado por la tesis: la utilización de un andamiaje constituye "una estrategia pedagógica eficaz para favorecer la elaboración de juicios de autoeficacia positivos, así como para reducir los niveles de carga cognitiva y mejorar el logro de aprendizaje". El andamiaje ayuda "a los sujetos dependientes de campo e independientes de campo equivalentemente", por lo que los ambientes computacionales con andamiaje motivacional favorecen un desempeño académico más equitativo entre estudiantes con diferente estilo cognitivo DIC.
requirements: Incluir módulos que permitan al estudiante elegir metas, autoevaluarse y recibir mensajes motivacionales dentro del ambiente computacional
Diseñar el ambiente para reducir la carga extrínseca y favorecer la carga germánica
constraints: La tesis advierte que sus resultados "no son concluyentes" y, por el diseño cuasi-experimental con grupos preconformados, "no podrían ser generalizadas para el sistema educativo"
target_learners: Estudiantes de básica primaria con diferente estilo cognitivo DIC, especialmente dependientes de campo
target_learning_goals: Mejorar el logro de aprendizaje en matemáticas
Favorecer juicios de autoeficacia positivos
examples: En el estudio, los dependientes de campo mejoraron su alcance del logro con el andamiaje, disminuyendo las diferencias entre estilos cognitivos

article_title: A generative theory of textbook design: Using annotated illustrations to foster meaningful learning of science text
citation: Mayer, R.E., Steinhoff, K., Bower, G., & Mars, R. (1995). A generative theory of textbook design: Using annotated illustrations to foster meaningful learning of science text. ETR&D, 43, 31-41. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02300480

description: When designing illustrated science text, incorporate annotations — captions and labels repeating the verbal cause-and-effect information from the text — into the illustrations. The article found the transfer benefit of integrated illustrations "depended on incorporating annotations (i.e., captions and labels) into the illustrations rather than placing illustrations close to corresponding paragraphs."

constraints: Evidence comes from college students reading an explanatory text about lightning; benefit was weaker for learners with high domain experience

examples: The integrated group's illustrations were placed adjacent to corresponding text paragraphs and contained annotations repeating the verbal cause-and-effect information from the text about lightning formation.

citation: Hyde, D. C., Khanum, S., & Spelke, E. S. (2014). Brief non-symbolic, approximate number practice enhances subsequent exact symbolic arithmetic in children. Cognition, 131(1), 92-107. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2013.12.007

description: The article evaluates three families of accounts for the ANS-mathematics link: ANS-specific dependence, a generalized magnitude system spanning dimensions, and mediation by general cognitive operations such as comparison, ordering, or inhibitory control. Its experimental pattern supports the first: "our data provide evidence that symbolic arithmetic draws on at least some overlapping cognitive and/or neural structures used to represent approximate number." Non-numerical magnitude training with the same operations did not produce the enhancement, and effects were mathematics-specific.

article_title: Is approximate number precision a stable predictor of math ability?
citation: Libertus Melissa E., Feigenson Lisa, Halberda Justin. (2013). Is Approximate Number Precision a Stable Predictor of Math Ability? Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2013.02.001
title: Approximate Number System (ANS): a noisy, ratio-dependent system for representing numerical magnitudes
description: The Approximate Number System is described as a system for representing numerical information "using noisy mental magnitudes that are normally distributed around the number to be represented." Its hallmark is that representational noise increases with numerosity, so discrimination success depends on the ratio between two numerosities rather than their absolute difference, yielding Weber's Law behavior. The article measures individual ANS acuity via a psychophysical model estimating each participant's Weber fraction w, and treats acuity as improving across development while varying considerably between individuals of the same age.
requirements: Measurement via a non-symbolic numerical comparison task with trials spanning multiple numerical ratios to estimate the Weber fraction
constraints: The article notes ANS proficiency alone is not sufficient to generate formal math concepts, since infants and non-human animals show ANS representations without formal math skill
target_learning_goals: non-symbolic numerical estimation and discrimination
early mathematics ability
examples: The study estimated each child's Weber fraction w from 60 test trials using maximum likelihood estimation over a Gaussian model of numerosity representations

article_title: The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts
citation: van der Pol, J., Admiraal, W., & Simons, P.R.J. (2006). The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 1(3), 339–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-9657-6
title: Anchored discussion: linked artifact-centered discourse creating a stronger collaborative context
description: Anchored discussion is a design for online discussion in which the article under discussion is displayed adjacent to the threaded discussion and messages can be anchored to specific passages of the text. Unlike shared annotation, which starts from personal notes made visible to peers, anchored discussion "starts from the notion of collaborative discussion that is contextualized or 'anchored' within a specific content," displaying "both artifact and discussion in a linked, yet independent manner." The article argues this document-centeredness defines a stronger collaborative context that focuses participants' collaborative intentions and gives messages a stronger frame of reference, reducing the effort needed for grounding and clarification.
requirements: The discussion environment must physically present the text online adjacent to the threaded discussion and allow anchoring messages to specific passages of the text.
constraints: The article notes technical issues with the studied system (such as the placement of certain buttons) that should be resolved in further development.

The observed advantages concern the early stages of collaborative literature processing by undergraduates; for more personal and critical discussion among participants with sufficient understanding, the authors suggest traditional forum discussion might be better suited.
target_learners: Undergraduate students processing academic literature in higher education
target_learning_goals: Collaborative comprehension and processing of academic texts
examples: In the study, 18 student groups in a first-year pedagogy course discussed two articles over two-week rounds, half in the anchored system and half in a Blackboard forum, producing 1,133 task-related messages.

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Analyze educational technology use from the participants' perspective rather than imposing preconceived codes
description: Stahl argues EM rejects coding schemes, predefined hypotheses, and researcher-imposed frameworks; instead research should use thick description to analyze what learners make mean, what participants can see, and how they display mutual meaning as accountable. In CSCL this means studying learner actions and discourse from the learner's perspective without pre-structuring analysis.
requirements: Data must include naturally occurring interaction (transcripts, logs, recordings) with sufficient detail to display participants' own accountability of meaning
constraints: Limits generalization: single case studies; analysis validity depends on data sessions and consensual reader-check by experienced analysts
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning: understanding interaction and meaning making from participants' own perspective
examples: Stahl describes how EM researchers use detailed transcripts so readers can validate the analysis via their own cultural understanding

article_title: When learning from animations is more successful than learning from static pictures: learning the specifics of change
citation: Rolf Ploetzner, Sandra Berney, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2021). When learning from animations is more successful than learning from static pictures: learning the specifics of change. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09541-w
title: Animation Process Model (APM): five interacting phases of perceptual and cognitive processing in learning from unnarrated animations
description: The Animation Process Model (APM; Lowe & Boucheix, 2008, 2011; Lowe & Schnotz, 2014) describes how learning from unnarrated animations progresses through five phases in which "perceptual bottom-up and cognitive top-down processes interact". Learners first identify confined event units, merge them into dynamic micro-chunks, combine these into relational structures such as causal chains, associate functional tasks yielding functional episodes, and finally refine the established functionality. The phases are not processed in linear order, and learners with little prior knowledge must repeatedly apply the processes. The article uses the APM to argue that perceptual-level learning is an educational objective in its own right and focused its study on perceptual processing.
requirements: Learners must sufficiently perceive and comprehend the animation for it to be educationally effective; learners with little prior knowledge need repeated processing of the phases
constraints: The article notes it remains to be described in detail how perceptual processes during learning from animations facilitate conceptual understanding and vice versa
target_learners: undergraduate pre-service teacher students learning from unnarrated animations
novice learners with little prior knowledge of the animated subject matter
target_learning_goals: constructing mental representations of displayed changes and how they unfold in time (kinematic models)
perceptual learning of motion patterns and spatial arrangements
examples: The experimental study focused on perceptual processing during learning from animation, using motion- and arrangement-identification tasks with proximity to perceptual memory tasks

description: The article implements and tests an analytical approach to strategy training that "combined a detailed, step-by-step presentation of each strategy with the integration of various strategies across modules and practice tasks." description: The article adapts ANT into a recursive analytic procedure for classroom talk with seven steps: recognizing actors (human and non-human), tracing connections into assemblages, identifying translations of roles, identifying shifts and changes in the network, delineating interactions' outcomes, examining connections to other networks, and revealing black boxes. citation: Bicakci, M., Heller, F., Stoeger, H., & Ziegler, A. (2026). From RAMSing to Rigor: Improving Moderator Analysis in STEM Education Meta-Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10172-1

description: The authors developed "a comprehensive toolkit, implemented as fully annotated R scripts and accompanied by a worked example dataset, which is publicly available on the Open Science Framework." description: In closing, the report endorses Külppe's observation that "the fundamental principle of modern instruction, the principle of emphasis on sense perception (Anschauung), is in need of revision." citation: Abigail Gurin Schleifer, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Giora Alexandron. (2025). Uncovering Measurement Biases in LLM Embedding Spaces: The Anna Karenina Principle and Its Implications for Automated Feedback. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00485-7
title: The Anna Karenina Principle in Automated Short Answer Scoring
description: The Anna Karenina (AK) principle in ASAS is the authors' explanatory account of why embeddings-based clustering of student responses favors correct answers: correct responses ('happy families') are densely and similarly represented, whereas incorrect responses ('unhappy families') "tend to differ from each other", increasingly so the more severe the error. The strong version adds that incorrect responses sit closer to correct ones than to their own profile, so correct responses are "the center of the universe". Lower density and non-convexity of poor-knowledge profiles are proposed as inhibitors of downstream discoverability, yielding a measurement bias against lower-knowledge learners.
requirements: Pre-trained LLM embeddings of student responses and a theory-driven profile labeling to diagnose the geometry
constraints: Demonstrated in the context of ASAS with LLM embeddings on Hebrew biology explanation responses; the authors note it may be fundamental to educational assessment but call for dedicated study
target_learning_goals: constructing scientific explanations
diagnosis of error patterns for formative feedback
examples: Within-KP cosine similarity medians fell monotonically with KP index across three embedding models; incorrect responses' nearest high-density region was KP1

title: Five-Category Answer Categorization Scheme Based on Completeness and Accuracy
description: A student's answer is characterized in terms of completeness and accuracy, yielding five categories: Incomplete-Accurate (IncAcc), Incomplete-Inaccurate (IncIna), Complete-Inaccurate (ComIna), Complete-Accurate (ComAcc), and Superfluous (SF). An answer is complete if all nodes of the correct answer appear in the student's answer; it is accurate when all its nodes are correct. description: The article's main design implication is that integrating external tools in MOOCs involves a trade-off: the most seamless design lets learners use the tool anonymously with no extra registration, while requiring registration (an extra commitment step) unlocks persistence features such as saved progress. The authors "suggest the need for a trade-off between designing MOOCs that allow a very easy and anonymous access to external tools aimed for a more active learning, and forcing learners to give a step forward in terms of commitment in exchange for benefitting from additional features".

title: Antecedents–processes–consequences framework for CSCL research
description: The article argues that fundamental understanding of CSCL requires simultaneously studying antecedents (student-, group-, task-, and technological characteristics), processes (descriptions and qualities of interactions and individual learning activities during collaboration), and consequences (e.g., individual achievement, group performance, perceived efficacy) of collaboration, and whether processes mediate antecedents' effects on consequences. Table 2 enumerates the antecedent elements, such as prior knowledge, group size, task complexity, and availability of collaboration scripts, scaffolds, and awareness tools.

constraints: Most prior research has focused on the relation between antecedents and consequences, neglecting the process of collaboration itself

examples: The article's Fig. 1 depicts the relationship between antecedents, processes, and consequences of collaboration

title: Analogous-students method for computing individual normalized gains across non-overlapping cohorts.
description: Because the same students did not experience both methodologies, the authors introduced the “analogous students” concept: students in the FT and TM groups occupying the same position in a lab-grade ranking within low/high grade subgroups are paired, and the individual normalized gain gi is computed for each FT student from the paired TM student's grade. The introduction of the concept allowed the authors “to associate confidence intervals with the results of the gain and perform a more robust statistical study.” Random exclusion balanced unequal subgroup sizes, giving a final sample of 613 students.
requirements: Two-step procedure: divide groups into low and high levels by total course grade, then rank by laboratory grades within each subgroup for each course and pair same-position students.
constraints: When subgroup sizes differed between methodologies, some students were excluded randomly from the subgroup with most members; the method assumes grade ranks are comparable across cohorts.

target_learning_goals: measuring knowledge gained between teaching methodologies
examples: Applied to Physics (299 students) and Electricity (314 students) cohorts from 2013-2017, producing individual gains gi mostly between 0 and 0.2.

title: Schedule mandatory annual or semiannual BLS refresher sessions rather than one-off interventions, because knowledge deteriorates within months
description: A design recommendation for school health programming derived from the review's retention findings. Because most studies show BLS knowledge decays quickly, the review states that "school health programs should incorporate mandatory annual or semiannual refresher sessions into the curriculum rather than relying on one‐off interventions." requirements: Refresher sessions must be built into the school curriculum as mandatory rather than optional additions.

examples: The review found most studies confirm knowledge of BLS deteriorates rapidly within a matter of months, motivating the refresher recommendation.

description: A scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley five-stage framework and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines, prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework. The search of six databases and two major dental education journals up to May 2024 identified 1412 records, of which "ten articles were selected after screening", with substantial inter-rater agreement (Kappa 0.78). The included studies span eight countries, undergraduate and licensure contexts, and MCQ, SAQ and OSCE assessment formats, analysed through quantitative frequency and qualitative thematic analysis using NVivo 12.

examples: Most included studies used retrospective designs, with only one prospective study (Schoonheim-Klein et al., Netherlands)

title: Angoff methods as a flexible family of standard-setting approaches
description: The article frames the Angoff method not as a single technique but as "a flexible family of approaches with distinct outcomes." The family includes Traditional Angoff, Modified Angoff, Angoff (Yes/No), Angoff Group (Yes/No), Three-level Angoff, and Mastery Angoff, each differing in how judges estimate borderline candidate performance. The choice of variant allows for the deliberate setting of more lenient or stringent standards, making variant selection a conscious decision aligned with assessment purpose and context.

constraints: An uninformed choice of variant can lead to unintended pass rates.

citation: Kang Jiamin, Hu Jiale, Yan Chunji, Xing Xueyan, Tu Shumin, Zhou Fang. (2024). Development and applications of the Anaesthetists’ Non-Technical Skills behavioural marker system: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2023-075019
title: The ANTS behavioural marker system: four skill categories with 15 elements rated on 4-point Likert scales
description: The ANTS behavioural marker system is a framework developed and tested by Fletcher et al at the University of Aberdeen in 2002 for training and evaluating anaesthetists' performance. It "includes four skill categories necessary for good anaesthetic practice, including task management, teamwork, situation awareness and decision-making, with 15 elements and examples of good and bad behaviours for each element". It uses "a set of 4-point Likert scales to rate observed behaviours" with space for open comments, and supplies a common language for discussing non-technical skills and a framework for structuring teaching and debriefing.
requirements: Raters should conduct calibration and training in the system before using it for teaching and evaluation to ensure standardised judgement, as emphasised in the ANTS handbook
Assessment should be based only on behaviours observed directly, rated first at element level and then at the more general category level
constraints: The system cannot differentiate between NTS required for different scenarios and cannot capture and evaluate short scenarios
It does not distinguish between NTS required in a particular clinical setting and NTS in general
Over-reliance on assessment of the measure in the original study and failure to re-establish validity when modified or assessed in a new population or scenario
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills: task management, teamwork, situation awareness and decision-making
examples: Adapted NTS behavioural marker systems were developed for an organ procurement team, nurse anaesthetists and medical air ambulance teams using ANTS as the starting point

article_title: Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge.
citation: Mickenautsch Steffen. (2010). Systematic reviews, systematic error and the acquisition of clinical knowledge. BMC Medical Research Methodology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-10-53
title: Analysis-synthesis unity model of clinical knowledge acquisition
description: The article proposes a model in which clinical knowledge acquisition depends on the interaction between analytic and synthetic processes rather than their opposition. Analytic knowledge from basic science and experience forms the basis for plausible hypothesis development, which is then tested through synthesis by trial, and systematic reviews unify isolated trial results. The article states that "The acquisition of clinical knowledge is based on the interaction between analysis and synthesis" and that systematic reviews inform the analytic knowledge of the clinician without replacing it.
requirements: A plausible hypothesis developed through analysis must precede hypothesis testing through synthesis
constraints: The article presents this as a philosophical proposition rather than an empirically tested model

examples: The article illustrates the model with the ART approach in dentistry: GV Black's extension for prevention concept as thesis, Mertz-Fairhurst's observation as antithesis, and Frencken's synthesis through selective caries removal

article_title: Exploring the Impacts of Analogies on Computer Hardware
citation: Dincer, S. (2011). Exploring the Impacts of Analogies on Computer Hardware. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Theory of analogical reasoning as mapping between familiar and new structures
description: The article presents analogical reasoning as a complex cognitive process in which elements and relationships of a familiar domain are mapped onto a new target domain. Mapping compares knowledge already in long-term memory with ongoing interaction and empirical observations engaging sensory memory, with working memory serving as the arena for linking familiar and new structures. The article states that "as a result of analogical reasoning, there can be an emergence of an enriched internal cognitive representation or mental model which may be subsequently stored in long-term memory". Three hypotheses follow: analogies provide a familiar basis for new concepts, reasoning is supported by dynamic correlation between new and familiar structural relations, and an enriched mental model can be generated.
requirements: Students' analogical reasoning, correlation reasoning, and visual imagery must not be constrained for analogy use to be effective
constraints: Use of analogies is limited when students' analogical or correlation reasoning or visual imagery is constrained, and when students cannot map the familiar onto new phenomena
target_learners: learners encountering abstract, unobservable science and computing concepts
target_learning_goals: conceptual change and construction of mental models for unobservable phenomena
examples: The study applied this mapping account by mapping human organs, a workbench, and bus bridges onto hardware, RAM, and logic gates respectively

title: Analogy-based corrective feedback as an exemplar-based strategy combining recast and explicit correction with a repair prompt
description: Analogy-based corrective feedback is defined as a feedback strategy in which the teacher "provides a structurally similar synonymous example to an erroneous learner utterance where that form is corrected and also includes a prompt for learner revision" (Thomas, 2018, as quoted in the article). It is described as an amalgamation of recast plus explicit correction: the learner receives both positive and negative evidence in one move, and a repair prompt pushes the learner to find and fix the error, producing uptake. The article treats it as the exemplar-based counterpart to rule-based metalinguistic feedback and tests it in communicative tasks with young EFL learners.
requirements: The teacher must prepare a repair prompt that pushes the student to find and fix their error, as in the article's classroom example
constraints: The article notes the method has a difficult nature in oral classrooms and a "potential difficulty of spontaneously producing" the analogous example (Thomas, 2018, p. 18)
target_learners: young EFL learners at elementary level (ages 10-13)
target_learning_goals: grammar target structures such as yes/no questions, conditionals and prepositions
examples: In the article's classroom extract, after the learner says "when...she go afternoon", the teacher models "she writes a letter" and asks the learner to correct the sentence with their original words, and the learner produces "she goes to the party in the afternoon"

article_title: Mind the Gap: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary

title: Mind the Gap animation course (Animate Learning): five facilitated family workshops creating an animated film with an explicit metacognitive focus
description: The animation project is the parental engagement component of Mind the Gap: "five sessions (10 hours in total , 2 hours per week for 5 weeks ) where children and their parents worked together to create an animated film", usually after the school day and coordinated by a CfL-trained practitioner who helped participants reflect on how they were learning. Schools need the required IT hardware; delivery for up to 15 families costs in the region of £1,950, roughly £130 per child
constraints: The requirement for a class teacher to be present was not always met, due to varying levels of commitment and capacity

Fidelity challenges arose from changes in school staff and school-specific factors such as scheduling, the allocated staff member's role, the classroom environment, and communication about the project

home-school relationships and family learning
literacy and digital literacy skills

article_title: Immersive Planetarium Visualizations for Teaching Solar System Moon Concepts to Undergraduates
citation: Yu, K. C., Sahami, K., Denn, G., Sahami, V., & Sessions, L. C. (2016). Immersive Planetarium Visualizations for Teaching Solar System Moon Concepts to Undergraduates. Journal of Astronomy & Earth Sciences Education, 3(2). https://www.thecluteinstitute.com
title: Anatomy of disciplinary discernment as a scaffold for visualization-based astronomy instruction
description: Eriksson and colleagues' hierarchical framework, in which disciplinary discernment is "noticing something, reflecting on it, and constructing meaning from a disciplinary perspective," arranged from recognizing or naming objects in an astronomical representation, to assigning disciplinary meaning, to combining disciplinary elements into holistic understanding, to analyzing and critiquing the representation. The article uses this framework to structure its planetarium lecture as a purposefully constructed scaffold: simplest tasks involve identifying and naming planetary moons, while more sophisticated tasks combine principles (independent orbits, gravitational capture, accretion, impact ejection) into holistic understanding of scenarios for moon formation.
requirements: An instructor-guided tour through astronomical visualizations so learners can cross into increasingly advanced levels of discernment
constraints: The framework is applied here only to undergraduate moon concepts in introductory astronomy; the article does not claim it was tested as a variable
target_learning_goals: disciplinary discernment about planetary moons, including their identities, motions, and formation scenarios
examples: The moon lecture moved students from naming moons toward combining orbital and gravitational principles into holistic accounts of moon formation

article_title: Achievement Network's Investing in Innovation Expansion: Impacts on Educator Practice and Student Achievement
citation: Martin R. West, Beth A. Morton, Corinne M. Herlihy. (2016). Achievement Network's Investing in Innovation Expansion: Impacts on Educator Practice and Student Achievement. Center for Education Policy Research, Harvard University. http://cepr.harvard.edu
title: ANet's data-based instructional program model: interim assessments, data tools, leader coaching, and peer networks organized around a data cycle
description: ANet is a school-level intervention built on the belief that timely interim assessment data, leader support and structures, and teacher knowledge of how to help struggling students will make educators more effective at closing learning gaps. During the evaluation it had "four key components": quarterly standards-aligned interim assessments in math and ELA for Grades 3-8, data tools with individual student progress reports via the MyANet platform, coaching of school leaders, and a geographic network of peer schools sharing results and joint professional development. Its work is organized around a data cycle whose key leverage point is data review and action planning meetings, with coaches initially partnering with leaders who are then expected to take ownership. The logic model was later revised to add school structures as a key mediator and renamed the teaching and learning cycle.
requirements: School leaders must establish a data leadership team, schedule time for data meetings and re-teaching, align the assessment cycle to curricular resources, and maintain a student data system supporting the data cycle.
constraints: The evaluation sample consisted of schools deemed minimally ready and willing to commit discretionary budget, so findings generalize only to similarly equipped and motivated schools.
target_learners: students in Grades 3-8 in high-poverty schools
target_learning_goals: improving student achievement in math and reading through standards-aligned, data-based instruction
examples: Coaches visited schools roughly 20 times per academic year; after each assessment ANet returned results within two business days and coaches met leaders, data teams, and teachers in data meetings, typically three-hour blocks where teachers analyzed data and designed re-teaching plans.

article_title: The Effects of Analogy on Students' Understanding of Direct Current Circuits and Attitudes towards Physics Lessons
citation: Gokhan Ugur, Refik Dilber, Yasemin Senpolat, Bahattin Duzgun. (2012). The Effects of Analogy on Students' Understanding of Direct Current Circuits and Attitudes towards Physics Lessons. European Journal of Educational Research, 1(3), 211-223. http://www.akademikplus.com/eujer/index.html
title: Analog-target mapping theory: analogies aid learning when shared attributes are mapped, but unshared attributes cause impaired learning
description: The article frames analogy as "a process of identifying similarities between two concepts", with the familiar concept called the analog and the unfamiliar science concept the target. Shared attributes support the concept being taught, while unshared attributes can be wrongly mapped, producing impaired learning or misconceptions. It distinguishes superficial appearance matches, which "produce little growth in knowledge", from true inductive analogies sharing higher-order causative relations, which promote deep understanding but are difficult for unskilled learners.

Care is needed to ensure an impression is not conveyed that the analog is a true description of the target concept
constraints: If the analog is unfamiliar to the learner, development of systematic understanding is precluded
Students lacking visual imagery may be limited in analogical reasoning, and analogies may add unnecessary information or noise for students already at a formal operational level
target_learning_goals: Understanding of direct current circuit concepts
Elimination of misconceptions about electric circuits
examples: The study used six analogies including train, aquarium, u-pipe and water circuits-electric circuit analogies, some shown with physical tools and others drawn on the blackboard.

article_title: Comparison of examination performance and test anxiety during bell-paced and self-paced gross anatomy laboratory examinations.
citation: Bentley DC, Sotto A, Lombardi P. Comparison of examination performance and test anxiety during bell‐paced and self‐paced gross anatomy laboratory examinations. Anat Sci Educ. 2026;19:732–742. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70215
title: Anticipatory, consequent, and reactive test anxiety metrics for temporally disaggregated measurement of test anxiety.
description: The article proposes three novel, operationally defined test anxiety metrics to address inconsistent measurement in the field. Anticipatory test anxiety is the acute anxiety one experiences in advance of an assessment, measured with the state-specific portion of the STAI directly prior to beginning such an assessment. Consequent test anxiety is the acute anxiety one experiences following an assessment, measured with the same instrument after completion. Reactive test anxiety is the change in anxiety resulting from the assessment itself, calculated as consequent minus anticipatory test anxiety, where a positive score indicates an anxiety-inducing test environment.
requirements: State-specific STAI scores collected at matched pre-exam and post-exam timepoints for each assessment.
constraints: The article notes that the term test anxiety lacks precision and temporal granularity in the field, and that these metrics were developed by the authors' research group for this study context.
target_learning_goals: reducing test anxiety during high-stakes practical assessments
examples: The study measured STAI scores before and after both midterm and final laboratory examinations under two pacing conditions, then computed reactive test anxiety as the pre-to-post difference.

Pre–post changes in operating room nurses’ knowledge and attitudes toward medical device–related pressure injuries after a problem-based and simulation-based training program: a single-group pretest–posttest study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09147-1
title: Anchor nurse training in authentic, workflow-embedded clinical problems rather than general didactic content
description: The article argues that general, ward-oriented, compliance-focused training leaves OR nurses unable to translate recommendations into situationally appropriate intraoperative actions, and that its own hybrid program anchored learning in OR-specific device-risk scenarios. The authors state that "Problem-based learning (PBL) promotes active, case-driven learning and can strengthen nurses’ ability to identify device-related risks, prioritize prevention strategies, and justify decisions in complex perioperative cases."
requirements: Case triggers describing patient characteristics, surgical position, expected duration, applied devices, and operational constraints
constraints: Evidence comes from a single-group pretest–posttest study without a control group; gains are associations, not causal effects
target_learning_goals: Device-related risk identification
Prevention planning and clinical reasoning
examples: PBL sessions used OR-specific MDRPI vignettes covering devices such as positioning pads, electrode patches, and pulse oximetry probes

article_title: Exploring the impact of virtual reality anatomy training on preparing biomedical illustrators for drawing anatomical structures.
citation: Cheung H. C. Kristy, Zhong Lily Shengjia, Wall Shelley L., Lisk Kristina. (2026). Exploring the impact of virtual reality anatomy training on preparing biomedical illustrators for drawing anatomical structures. Anatomical Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/ase.70150
title: Illustration scoring rubric adapted from a validated medical visualization scale with five criteria
description: An illustration scoring rubric created as an adaptation of a validated medical visualization scale, with five evaluation criteria: "layout, visual clarity, style, hierarchy and anatomical accuracy." Each criterion has five rating levels with short performance descriptions, and the rubric was reviewed and modified by two subject matter experts. Two experts scored all 51 illustrations independently; interrater reliability was ICC 0.64 (95% CI: 0.44–0.78) for composite scores and moderate agreement (BPC 0.62–0.79) across components.
requirements: Scoring by subject matter experts with anonymized illustrations; rubric review by two experts for alignment with the application
constraints: Interrater agreement was moderate rather than high (ICC 0.64; BPC 0.62–0.79 across components)
target_learning_goals: producing anatomical illustrations that accurately depict spatial relationships and depth of anatomical structures
examples: Used to score 51 illustrations from the crossover study, revealing modality differences in hierarchy and layout components

citation: Liu Ganwei, Yang Feng, Zhou Zuli, Jiang Guanchao. (2025). A Novel Competency-Based Simulation Model for Thoracoscopic Lung Resection. The Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgeon. https://doi.org/10.1055/a-2702-2239
title: Integrate anatomically accurate, high-fidelity simulation as a core element of thoracic surgical education rather than an optional adjunct
description: The article argues that because VATS has a steep learning curve and many residents lack independent operative exposure, "simulation should not be considered an optional adjunct but rather a core element of surgical education." High-fidelity models permit repeated practice of dissection, stapling, and spatial navigation in a risk-free environment, and the study's randomized comparison supports their advantage over generic box trainers for procedure-specific learning.
requirements: Anatomical fidelity and tactile realism matched to the target procedure
Grounding in sound pedagogical principles such as deliberate practice with structured feedback
constraints: Live animal and synthetic models still differ from human anatomy and cannot fully capture intraoperative variability; cost-effectiveness and logistical feasibility across institutions warrant further exploration
target_learning_goals: anatomical understanding
technical skill acquisition
clinical readiness and confidence
examples: The randomized trial assigned 52 residents to lung-model or FLS training and assessed transfer in live animal surgery one week later

description: Anatomy Interactives is a web-based laboratory manual built in iSpring Suite to complement prosection laboratories for MD, PA, and DPT students. It contains "interactive labeled images, donor photographs, and quiz-style self-assessments", organized into six regional laboratories from back and upper limb to head and neck. Modules pair hover-over identification resources with donor-based pin-on-image, multiple-choice, and check-all-that-apply tasks providing formative feedback, and are hosted on the institution's learning management system for on-demand access.

A device that connects to the internet
constraints: Module progression is modeled after the University of Kentucky's gross anatomy curriculum and may not directly follow other institutions' curricula

Preparation for written and laboratory examinations

PA/DPT students used the modules as self-study before laboratories and assessments

citation: Kldiashvili E., Al-Rustum S., Zarnadze M., Goderdzishvili D., Tvildiani M., Mamiseishvili A. (2025). Application of project-based and simulation-based approaches in medical curriculum. BMC Medical Education 25:1707. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08196-2
title: Anatomage-table virtual case analysis as a simulation-based case-report assignment
description: The Anatomage Table is used in this study as a simulation platform on which students explore virtual 3D clinical cases "based on real anonymized radiologic data." A bank of cases was preloaded and thematically categorized (e.g., trauma, oncology, cardiology); each student selected a unique case, analysed clinical findings, formed differential diagnoses, and prepared an academic case report within 14 days after orientation on case analysis and report structure. It served as the intervention arm (Group D, n = 43) against paper-based case preparation, supporting both case understanding and written-report quality.
requirements: Orientation sessions providing guidance on case analysis, diagnostic frameworks, and report structure
Completion of basic science coursework before use
constraints: Students in this study had no prior Anatomage experience, so novelty effects cannot be ruled out
The small simulation-component sample and single-institution context may limit generalizability
target_learning_goals: Clinical case analysis and differential diagnosis
Academic case-report writing and science communication
examples: Group D students explored preloaded virtual 3D clinical cases on the Anatomage Table and prepared academic case reports in 14 days, compared with Group C's paper-based case reports

title: Use anterior alpha-band group EEG synchronization as an objective complement to subjective TeamSTEPPS assessment in virtual simulation-based interprofessional education
description: The article proposes group anterior alpha-band total interdependence as a complement to rater-based TeamSTEPPS evaluation in online virtual SIMBIE, where "assessing situation monitoring and mutual support with human raters is inherently limited by the subjectivity required to evaluate nonverbal behaviors". The authors conclude that "anterior alpha TI may serve as an objective metric for assessing TeamSTEPPS-based team performance", with potential for automatic, real-time feedback.
requirements: Wireless EEG recording from all team members during virtual simulation sessions, with computation of normalized group total interdependence for the anterior alpha band (8-12 Hz).
constraints: Evidence is correlational, from a single-center study of 30 six-person sessions; the group-level negative correlation coexists with null individual-level correlations, and posterior all-band TI shows positive correlations with most domains.
target_learners: multiprofessional health care students (medical, nursing, pharmacy, medical technology, radiological technology) in virtual simulation-based interprofessional education
target_learning_goals: teamwork and communication performance assessment across TeamSTEPPS domains in crisis simulation
examples: In the study, 2 trained raters independently rated each profession's TeamSTEPPS performance from screen recordings while wireless EEG was recorded from all 6 participants, and group anterior alpha TI was correlated with group TeamSTEPPS scores across all 5 domains and the overall score.

description: A live-tissue (porcine-model) simulation platform on which trainees perform complete endoscopic thyroidectomy procedures, including creating the working space, coagulating vessels, and identifying and preserving structures such as the parathyroid glands and laryngeal nerves. title: The Australia New Zealand Microsurgical Skills Course (ANZMSC)
description: The ANZMSC is a three-day ophthalmic microsurgical skills course conducted through the University of Sydney at the Sight for Life Foundation Surgical Skills Training Laboratory, running three times a year with twenty students per course. The article describes it as "the first ophthalmic microsurgical skills course in the Southern Hemisphere that has been made mandatory by RANZCO for first year ophthalmology trainees". It comprises eleven practical skills stations covering suturing on skills boards and pig eyes, strabismus surgery on model eyes and cadavers, eyelid repair and minor procedures on cadavers, and phacoemulsification on EyeSi simulators and dry lab sets, supported by pre-course online lectures and live demonstrations.

Course materials and equipment supplied by SFLSSTL and industry partners
constraints: Course fee of $2,750 AUD for participants, with reimbursement available in New Zealand but not typically in Australia

target_learning_goals: Ophthalmic microsurgical skills including corneal suturing, strabismus surgery, eyelid repair, and phacoemulsification

title: Undergraduate anesthesiology internship model with supervised and independent clinical shifts
description: A clinical education model in which final-term anesthesiology students who have reached appropriate competence complete some clinical courses with an instructor present and some independently in hospital wards, working under the direct supervision of an anesthesiologist and an anesthesia expert. In this implementation each student spent 51 hours per internship unit, with 60% of hours in the morning shift and 40% in evening plus night shifts in general and gynecological operating rooms. The article evaluates it via SWOT-based qualitative content analysis, finding both significant strengths and correctable weaknesses.

Direct supervision of an anesthesiologist and an anesthesia expert
Strong basic-course teaching so students acquire sufficient skills and knowledge before the internship

More difficult to apply in non-teaching hospitals

Professional identity and patient-centered care

description: Andragogy is Malcolm Knowles's theory of adult learning, developed throughout the second half of the 20th century as an alternative to child-oriented pedagogy. The report presents it for medical physics educators whose residents and graduate trainees are adult learners: "adults need to know why they need to learn something before engaging in an educational activity", are self-directed, bring prior experience as a learning resource, and are motivated internally. title: Anxiety as an interpretive threat signal rather than a primary emotion
description: The article's explanatory account of anxiety in simulation: drawing on the psychological literature, it frames “anxiety as a signal of threat” whose meaning depends on how learners interpret internal and external stimuli. title: Anchoring vignettes as a non-parametric correction for heterogeneous scale use in self-assessed personality traits
description: The article applies the non-parametric anchoring-vignette approach of King and colleagues to personality measurement. After self-assessment items such as "I am always prepared", respondents rate the same statements for fictive persons (a hairdresser, surgeon, firefighter, bus driver); vignette answers identify heterogeneity in scale use, and the self-assessment is recoded relative to the vignettes so that "respondents' answers are on the same scale". constraints: The anchors themselves may be subject to bias, e.g. students with hairdressers in their direct environment may judge hairdressers' traits differently
The sample of college students is not representative of the full Dutch population
Respondents who tie or misplace vignettes cannot always be assigned a unique recoded value

target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of non-cognitive skills (Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, Risk Preference) used to predict academic performance
examples: Students rated themselves and the fictive occupations on 7-point scales; vignette-corrected traits took 5 values based on where the self-assessment fell relative to the two vignettes

In this study two trained reviewers scored team-leader non-technical performance from video recordings using ANTS.

constraints: Leadership is not a separate category but incorporated into the team working domain
