article_title: In how many ways is the approximate number system associated with exact calculation?
citation: Pinheiro-Chagas Pedro, Wood Guilherme, Knops André, Krinzinger Helga, Lonnemann Jan, Starling-Alves Isabella, Willmes Klaus, Haase Vitor Geraldi. (2014). In How Many Ways is the Approximate Number System Associated with Exact Calculation? PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0111155
title: Multiple instantiations of the approximate number system forming a hierarchical association from discrimination to manipulation of magnitudes
description: The article proposes that the ANS is not a single uniformly measured capacity but has distinct instantiations — comparison, estimation and approximate calculation — that tap different computational processes over a common numerosity representation. These instantiations may form a hierarchy: "non-symbolic estimation and calculation could be intermediate steps between simple number discrimination and exact calculation". The authors support this with intercorrelations among the three acuity measures and mediation results showing comparison's effect on exact calculation operating through estimation and addition. Coefficient values increased from comparison to addition, which the authors speculate reflects summation of noise during more complex magnitude manipulation.
requirements: Measuring the ANS with multiple tasks, since a single task cannot index the supposedly unique system
constraints: The precise mechanisms of the different instantiations and their interaction are described as scarcely addressed in the literature and requiring future empirical study
Cross-sectional trajectories should be confirmed in longitudinal studies
target_learners: Children in first to sixth grade of formal schooling
target_learning_goals: Exact calculation and arithmetic achievement
Approximate magnitude processing
examples: The study operationalized the three instantiations as the internal Weber fraction (comparison) and coefficients of variation (estimation and addition) in 202 children

article_title: Training in laparoscopic colorectal surgery: a new educational model using specially embalmed human anatomical specimen.
citation: Slieker Juliette C., Theeuwes Hilco P., van Rooijen Göran L., Lange Johan F., Kleinrensink Gert-Jan. (2012). Training in laparoscopic colorectal surgery: a new educational model using specially embalmed human anatomical specimen. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-012-2158-y
title: Anubifix™-embalmed human colorectal training model with permanently colored anatomical landmarks
description: A human cadaveric training model for laparoscopic colorectal surgery in which a specimen embalmed with the Anubifix™ method retains flexibility and plasticity. After a midline laparotomy, "aorta and iliac arteries (dark red), superior mesenteric artery/vein and its branches (red/blue), inferior mesenteric artery/vein and its branches (red/blue), gonadal arteries (purple), and ureters (yellow)" were dissected and painted with formaldehyde-proof paint, and the abdominal wall was closed airtight so pneumoperitoneum could be created. Residents used it to mobilize bowel and expose central vessels and ureters under supervision.
requirements: An Anubifix™-embalmed specimen, formaldehyde-proof coloring paint, an airtight abdominal wall closure with a butyl rubber sheet, and standard laparoscopic equipment with CO2 pneumoperitoneum
constraints: The model lacks active bleeding, which the authors note "can be an issue, although the importance of active bleeding in a training model can be questioned"
target_learners: first- and second-year surgical residents in general surgery
target_learning_goals: three-dimensional laparoscopic colorectal anatomy
laparoscopic cognitive and motor skills
anatomical image interpretation
examples: Residents alternated the roles of operating surgeon and first assistant, mobilizing the small bowel and exploring left- and right-sided colorectal anatomy, locating segmental colonic anatomy and exposing central vessels and ureters

article_title: Learner feedback and educational outcomes with an internet-based ambulatory curriculum: a qualitative and quantitative analysis.
citation: Sisson SD, Rastegar DA, Hughes MT, Bertram AK, Yeh HC. (2012). Learner feedback and educational outcomes with an internet-based ambulatory curriculum: a qualitative and quantitative analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-55
title: Annual feedback-based curricular revision cycle combining content enrichment with website design changes
description: The curriculum operated a repeating annual cycle in which learners access content and provide feedback throughout the academic year, then "Curricular content is revised and website enhancements are designed annually based on learner feedback." Revisions made content more visual (more tables, figures, algorithms, images), increased pre/post test questions with explanatory answer text, added recap statements, a navigation map, and switched didactics from program control to learner control while retaining pretest-before-didactics and posttest-after-didactics sequencing.
requirements: A mechanism for learners to give free-text feedback and instructive-value ratings as a mandatory component of module completion
constraints: Factual content was also updated annually irrespective of feedback comments when necessitated by advances in the medical literature
target_learning_goals: ambulatory care medical knowledge
examples: Changes included adding a navigation map to each module (2007), changing didactic sections from program control to learner control (2007), and adding 1-page printable summaries for completed modules (2006)
key_sources: Sisson SD, Rastegar DA, Hughes MT, Bertram AK, Yeh HC. (2012). Learner feedback and educational outcomes with an internet-based ambulatory curriculum: a qualitative and quantitative analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-12-55
